rows.verified: Leptospirosis is a zoonotic infection caused by pathogenic bacteria of the genus Leptospira.
Wild and domestic mammals can carry leptospires and shed them in urine, including rodents, cattle and pigs.
Humans can be infected through direct animal-urine exposure or urine-contaminated water and environments.
Leptospires can enter through skin or mucous membranes, especially where skin is broken or waterlogged.
Higher-exposure groups include agricultural, veterinary, pest-control, construction and canal workers and people undertaking water sports.
Prevention includes handwashing, prompt wound cleaning, showering after exposure, protective clothing and waterproof wound coverings.
There is no available human vaccine against leptospirosis, although vaccination is available for some animals.
UKHSA uses PCR for acute direct detection and IgM serology later in illness; blood and urine are appropriate diagnostic samples.
Leptospirosis risk depends on animal reservoirs, water contamination, skin integrity, occupation, recreation, rainfall, geography and timing.
UKHSA leptospirosis evidence is exposure-, animal-, environment-, person-, laboratory- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.
Toxoplasmosis is caused by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii and can pass from mammals to humans.
Pregnant people and people with weakened immune systems are among the groups at greatest risk of serious consequences.
A small occupational and seasonal risk exists from infected sheep afterbirth and newborn lambs during lambing.
The parasite may be acquired from infected-cat faeces, contaminated soil or raw and undercooked meat.
Preventive measures include gloves for gardening, handwashing and thorough cleaning after handling raw meat.
Fruit and vegetables should be washed and meat, especially lamb, pork and venison, should be cooked thoroughly.
Most people recover without treatment, but treatment is commonly used in pregnancy, immune suppression, eye disease and affected newborns.
Toxoplasmosis is not acquired merely by stroking a cat, owning a cat or contact with an infected person.
Toxoplasmosis risk depends on food preparation, soil and cat-faeces exposure, pregnancy, immunity, animal contact and timing.
Toxoplasmosis evidence is exposure-, food-, animal-, pregnancy-, immune-status- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.
